nameStory: The name 'quince' comes from the ancient Greek city of Cydon in Crete, where these fragrant fruits were especially prized. The Romans called it 'malum cotoneum' (apple of Cydon), which evolved through Old French into our modern word 'quince'.
description: Quince is a small deciduous tree in the rose family that produces distinctively fragrant, golden-yellow fruits shaped like bumpy pears. The tree typically grows 10-15 feet tall with a somewhat gnarled, spreading habit. It's related to apples and pears but stands alone as the only member of its genus, making it quite special in the botanical world.

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Hard, bright golden-yellow fruits shaped like bumpy pears with an incredibly strong, sweet fragrance that can fill a room - you'll smell them before you see them clearly

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Large pale pink to white flowers, about 2 inches across with 5 rounded petals and prominent yellow stamens in the center, blooming in spring

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Oval leaves that are alternate (not opposite), with a smooth edge and fuzzy white undersides that feel soft like velvet

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Small tree with an irregular, somewhat twisted branching pattern and smooth gray-brown bark on older trunks

habitat: In New England, quince is rarely found in the wild but occasionally escapes cultivation near old homesteads and abandoned orchards. It prefers well-drained soils and full sun, often persisting in sunny edges of former farm properties or naturalized areas near historical sites.

seasonality.spring: Showy pale pink flowers appear in late spring after the leaves emerge, making the small tree quite ornamental and attracting bees and other pollinators.
seasonality.summer: Green fruits develop and leaves are full and lush, with the distinctive fuzzy white undersides visible when wind flips them over.
seasonality.fall: Fruits ripen to brilliant golden-yellow and become intensely fragrant, while leaves may turn yellow before dropping.
seasonality.winter: Bare branches show the characteristic irregular, somewhat gnarled growth pattern typical of older quince trees.

funFact: Quince fruits are so astringent and hard when raw that they'll make your mouth pucker worse than a green persimmon, but when cooked they transform into sweet, aromatic treats that smell like a mixture of apples, pears, and tropical flowers!
confusionNotes: The hard, bumpy golden fruits might be mistaken for mishappen pears, but quinces have that unmistakable intense fragrance and remain rock-hard even when ripe. Remember: if you can easily bite into it raw, it's not a quince!
contextualKnowledge: Don't confuse this true quince with 'flowering quince' (Chaenomeles), a thorny ornamental shrub commonly planted in yards. True quince is a small tree with edible fruit, while flowering quince is a spiny shrub grown mainly for its early spring flowers.
compareHints: As the only member of genus Cydonia, quince is unique, but it's most similar to its rose family cousins apples and pears. Unlike apples and pears, quince fruits are incredibly fragrant, always hard when ripe, and covered in fine fuzz when young, plus the tree stays much smaller with more irregular branching.
